text:
## What the projection says

I ran all three options through the full 2026–2050 projection (Frank's death in 2032, Joyce single from 2033, heirs' pre-tax IRA money valued at 22%, everything in today's dollars).

| Option | After-tax wealth at end (2026 $) | vs. no conversions |
|---|---|---|
| C — no conversions | $3,072,664 | — |
| A — convert 2033–2038 (after Frank's death) | $3,144,173 | +$71,510 |
| **B — convert 2026–2031 (while still filing jointly)** | **$3,328,935** | **+$256,272** |

**B wins clearly** — $184,762 ahead of A, and far outside the $1,000 "close call" band.

**Why B beats A.** The conversions are the same size (6 × $155,000 = $930,000), but the tax rate paid on them is not:

- Under **B**, the 2026–2031 conversions land in the **10%, 12% and 22% brackets** on a joint return — roughly $24,000–$25,000 of federal tax per $155,000 converted. Lifetime tax drops by $332,977 and lifetime Medicare by $46,004 versus C.
- Under **A**, the same $155,000 a year from 2033 is taxed in the **24%, 32% and 35% brackets** on Joyce's *single* return (only her $52,000 survivor Social Security and the joint IRA RMDs behind it), plus it pushes her into IRMAA tier 4. That plan actually *raises* her Medicare premiums in several years. Lifetime tax falls only $97,602.
- B also shrinks Joyce's pre-tax IRA to about $155,000 by 2032, so from 2033 onward her RMDs are tiny and she stays in a low bracket — the opposite of A, where her RMDs keep climbing and drag her into IRMAA tier 3–4 for two decades.

B is not free: 2026–2031 cost about $32,000 a year in extra federal tax, and the 2026 income lifts both spouses into IRMAA tier 1 for 2028 (about $2,400 more in premiums). But the tax savings later — on Joyce's single return and on what the heirs inherit — swamp that.

**N1 — 2026 federal tax, B vs. C:** $33,282 − $1,041 = **$32,241** (about $24,774 from the $155,000 itself at 10/12/22%, $5,184 from more Social Security becoming taxable — the "tax torpedo" — and $2,283 from the senior deduction shrinking as MAGI passes $150,000).

**N2 — 2028 Medicare, B vs. C:** each spouse goes from tier 0 ($2,558/yr) to tier 1 ($3,764/yr), so 2 × $1,206 = **$2,412** more, set by the higher 2026 MAGI.

Two things that could move this: what return the accounts actually earn (a 7% return widens the gap by roughly $289,000 in B's favor), and the children's bracket (at 32% instead of 22%, B looks even better — the follow-ups rank heirs' bracket first).

PICK: B
N1: 32241
N2: 2412

Does Glen have a traditional IRA or employer plan, and what was its balance on December 31, 2025?

text:
## What the numbers say

I ran all three options through the full projection (2026–2050, both surviving to 91, 6% return, 2.5% inflation, heirs at 10%):

| Plan | After-tax wealth 12/31/2050 (2026 $) | vs. no conversion | Lifetime federal tax (2026 $) | Lifetime Medicare |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **C — no conversion** | 2,513,140 | — | 323,955 | 121,744 |
| **A — $190,000 × 3 yrs** | **2,516,844** | **+3,704** | 273,418 | 128,631 |
| **B — $195,500 × 3 yrs** | 2,512,691 | −450 | 275,083 | 128,631 |

**Option A wins**, by $3,704 over doing nothing and $4,153 over B. But be clear-eyed: a 0.15% edge over 25 years is a rounding error, not a slam dunk. Option B actually *loses* to doing nothing.

**Why A beats B:** the last $5,500 a year of B's conversion is taxed at 24% (A stops at the top of the 22% bracket), while the future rate it saves is only 12–22%. B also drags more Social Security into tax and pushes dividends out of the 0% capital-gain band. Beyond roughly $190,000 the conversion stops paying for itself.

**Why converting barely beats not converting:** Glen's RMDs at 73 are large (~$65k–$170k), but they land in the 12–22% brackets anyway — the same rates they'd pay to convert. So the conversion is close to a wash, with the benefit coming mostly from the smaller late-life RMDs and smaller IRMAA-driven premium bumps.

**Two things that would flip this:** at a 4% return, or if spending is really $140,400, **no conversion** becomes the best answer. If the heirs are in the 32% bracket, converting is worth about $92,000 more — that's the single biggest lever. Also note only ~11% of each conversion is tax-free (the $144,000 Form 8606 basis spread over a $1.2M IRA), and both A and B trip the first IRMAA tier for 2028–2030.

**On your two side questions:** the 2026 return under B shows $41,855 of federal tax versus $4,665 under C — a $37,190 jump for $195,500 of conversion, because the extra income kills the $12,000 senior deduction outright, makes $1,072 more Social Security taxable, taxes the dividends at 15% instead of 0%, and adds $772 of NIIT. For 2028 premiums, both plans' 2026 MAGI (B: $270,305; C: $95,682) put them one tier apart — $298.50 + $15.20 Part B/D versus the $213.20 standard, for both spouses, all 12 months.

PICK: A
N1: 37190
N2: 2412

text:
## Both claims are half right — and the half that's wrong is the one that matters

**Claim 1 ("the senior deduction makes these years good for converting") — right, but for a smaller reason than they think.** The deduction is $6,000 per spouse, phased out at 6% of MAGI over $150,000 *for each person separately*, and it disappears after 2028. So it is worth something — but its whole value is a deduction, not a credit: at their marginal rate the full $12,000 is worth roughly $2,600 of tax. That's a rounding error next to the brackets they're avoiding.

**Claim 2 ("converting can cost them that deduction") — true, and here is exactly what it costs.** Under option C their 2026 MAGI is $169,221, so each spouse loses $1,153.50 of the $6,000: the combined senior deduction falls from $12,000 to **$9,693**, and that $2,307 of lost deduction costs about **$507** of tax. Over 2027 and 2028 the phase-out costs $606 and $689. Total cost of the phase-out across the three conversion years: roughly **$1,800**. Total benefit of converting in those years: **$72,529**. The deduction is not a reason to wait; it's a rounding error on the invoice.

## The 2026 numbers they asked for

- **N1:** 2026 federal tax is **$6,620** with no conversion and **$16,311** under option C — **$9,691 more**. The engine's own breakdown of that $9,691: $8,328 from the extra taxable IRA distribution (the $65,000 conversion is only partly taxable — Ken's $131,000 of Form 8606 basis makes $56,719 of it income under the pro-rata rule), $507 from the senior-deduction phase-out, and $855 because the extra ordinary income pushes their qualified dividends out of the 0% capital-gain band. Note the "0% band" point: at their income the conversion doesn't just cost 12%/22% — it also costs the free treatment of their dividends.
- **N2:** the 2026 senior deduction under option C is **$9,693** ($4,846.50 each), not $12,000.

## Why C beats A — the timing is the whole argument

Both conversions are $195,000 total. Price them:

| | 2026 | 2027 | 2028 | 2029 | 2030 | 2031 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **C** federal tax | 16,311 | 16,768 | 17,048 | 10,149 | 10,831 | 11,552 |
| **A** federal tax | 6,620 | 7,211 | 7,774 | 24,198 | 24,823 | 25,421 |
| **B** federal tax | 6,620 | 7,211 | 7,774 | 11,356 | 12,771 | 14,172 |

- C's three conversion years cost **$28,522** of extra tax over doing nothing — about **14.6%** per dollar converted.
- A's three conversion years cost **$36,143** — about **18.5%** per dollar converted.

Waiting is more expensive because 2029 is when **Gail's own RMDs begin** (she turns 73 in 2029, adding $13,034 on top of Ken's $44,860). Under option A the 2029 return already shows $202,069 of MAGI before any conversion, so the conversion stacks on top of a much higher base; under C, 2029 MAGI is only $133,960. Waiting also forfeits the senior deduction entirely — it's gone after 2028 — and by 2029 the taxable-account income has grown enough that A's 2029 conversion throws off $1,018 of extra dividend/gain tax that C avoids.

**And why convert at all:** with $1.26 million of pre-tax IRAs plus $390,000 of cash throwing off $23,400 of taxable interest, their RMDs and interest alone climb to where they cross into the 3.8% net investment income tax — B pays NIIT every year from 2039 on (peaking at $6,627 in 2050), and C shrinks that to $4,857. Lifetime federal tax (in today's dollars): B **$520,452**, A **$473,913**, C **$454,362**. After-tax wealth at the end of 2050 in today's dollars: B **$3,170,788**, A **$3,216,465**, C **$3,243,317**.

## Two things worth telling them

1. **No IRMAA cost, and no state tax.** 2026 MAGI of $169,221 is well under the $230,000 joint threshold that sets 2028 premiums, and every plan runs at IRMAA tier 0 in every year. So the conversion is priced only in income tax.
2. **$65,000 a year is more than they need to spend.** They had about $35,800 of room left in the 12% bracket in 2026; the last $29,000 of each conversion is being taxed at 22%. Among these three options C wins clearly — it beats A by $26,852 and B by $72,529, both far outside any rounding — but a conversion closer to $35,000–$40,000 a year would be cheaper per dollar than the $65,000 the options specify, if they want to revisit the amount. The one fact that would change this picture most is health/longevity (a long widowhood in the single brackets makes converting even more valuable; an early death cuts the benefit but doesn't reverse it).

PICK: C
N1: 9691
N2: 9693

text:
## What the numbers say

I ran the full 2026–2050 projection (5% returns, 2.5% inflation, no state tax, 12% heirs' rate) with every rule stacked in form order: RMDs starting for Ray in 2030 (age 73), the Social Security tax torpedo, the OBBBA senior deduction phasing out over $150,000 of MAGI, IRMAA two years back, and the pro‑rata rule on Ray's $208,000 of Form 8606 basis.

**Why converting pays at all.** Their 2026 baseline is tiny — AGI $75,064, taxable income $27,564, federal tax $2,812 — but that is a mirage. Ray's IRA is $1.6 million and his first RMD (2030) is about $73,389, which pushes AGI to $161,266 and federal tax to $15,205, and it keeps climbing to $63,080 by 2050. They also have $440,000 of cash earning taxable interest that compounds into the same bracket. So they are sitting in the 12% bracket today and heading for the 22–24% bracket permanently. Filling the 22% bracket now at roughly 21.6 cents per dollar beats paying 22–24% later — and beats the heirs' rate on whatever is left.

**The shape of the curve** (after-tax wealth gained, today's dollars, 8 conversion years):

| Per year | Gain |
|---|---|
| $0 | $0 |
| $60,000 | $87,857 |
| $100,000 | $127,060 |
| **$118,000** | **$134,445** |
| $130,000 | $125,818 |
| $150,000 | $111,996 |
| $200,000 | $110,526 |

The peak is $118,000 a year for 8 years (2026–2033), converting $944,000 in total, worth **+$134,445** in today's dollars. Beyond that the marginal dollars hit the 24% bracket ($180,217 of 2026 MAGI), then the senior-deduction cliff, the NIIT ($183,391) and IRMAA tier 1 ($153,702 → a $2,412 one-time cost for two people in 2028). Note the first-year break points: from $19,152 the torpedo is done and each dollar costs only 10.5 cents up to $67,306 — that cheap stretch is why even a small conversion helps — but the last dollar of the winning plan costs about 21.6 cents.

**Runner-up:** "stay just under the first IRMAA tier for 6 years" gets $133,853 — $592 less. So $118,000 × 8 is the pick, but anything in the $110,000–$155,000 range is essentially the same answer; it is not a knife-edge.

**N1.** Converting $155,000 in 2026 is only $135,810 taxable (pro-rata basis), and 2026 federal tax goes from $2,812 to $30,488 — **+$27,676**, made up of +$22,554 of ordinary income taxed at 12%/22%, +$3,138 of extra taxable Social Security (the torpedo), and +$1,984 from the senior deduction shrinking from $12,000 to $2,984.

**N2.** $155,000 of 2026 MAGI ($231,138) crosses the $218,000 joint threshold, so 2028 moves both spouses to IRMAA tier 1: $298.50 Part B + $15.20 Part D = $313.70/month versus $213.20 standard. That is $1,206 per person × 2 × 12 months = **$2,412**.

Two things would change the answer materially: the heirs' bracket (at 32% the optimum rises to $220,000 a year) and the actual expected return (at 7% it rises to $180,000 a year). I'd also want to confirm whether they intend any charitable giving — QCDs from age 70½ would substitute for some of these conversions at zero tax cost.

PLAN: 118000 x 8
N1: 27676
N2: 2412

text:
## What I did

I ran both options through the full 2026–2050 projection (5% returns, 2.5% inflation, RMDs on both IRAs — Sam's $26,792 and Pat's $14,118 for 2026 — IRMAA on 2024/2025 MAGI, the Social Security "tax torpedo," and the OBBBA senior deduction). The only differences between the two runs: under B the $11,000 comes out of Sam's traditional IRA as a QCD each year, and their own spending drops to $89,000 (no cash charitable gift, so the $2,000 non-itemizer charitable deduction goes away too).

## Why B wins

- **The QCD never enters income.** Under A, the $11,000 check is paid with money that was taxed on the way out of the IRA, and the gift buys them only the $2,000 non-itemizer charitable deduction (itemizing never gets close to their $37,500 standard deduction). Under B, the $11,000 leaves the IRA untaxed and still counts toward Sam's RMD (his 2026 RMD is $26,792, so the QCD fits comfortably inside it).
- **It shrinks the Social Security torpedo.** Their income sits in the 85%-inclusion zone, so each dollar of AGI avoided pulls about 85 cents of Social Security out of taxable income too. Taxable Social Security falls from $49,352 to $40,762 in 2026 alone.
- **2026 federal tax: $6,288 (A) vs $4,285 (B)** — $2,003 less, and the gap persists every year (lifetime federal tax $359,091 vs $336,153 in nominal dollars; $256,081 vs $237,090 in today's dollars).
- **It also drains the account the heirs would be taxed on.** The traditional IRA is worth only 76 cents on the dollar to heirs (24% rate); every QCD dollar avoids that forever, and the $11,000 they no longer spend stays in savings. Medicare premiums are identical in both plans (they stay in the base IRMAA tier either way).
- **Result:** after-tax wealth at the end of 2050 is **$1,149,924** under A versus **$1,261,282** under B (2026 dollars) — **$111,358 more with the QCD**. Not a close call.

One caveat worth noting: the QCD only works from Sam's IRA (he's over 70½), and it must be sent directly by the custodian to the church — a check to the church from a personal account doesn't count.

PICK: B

## What the numbers say

**First, the mechanics of Pat's inherited IRA.** Because the parent died in 2023 *after* their required beginning date, Pat — a non-eligible designated beneficiary under the 10-year rule — must take annual RMDs in 2024–2033 and empty the account by the end of 2033. The divisor is Pat's single life expectancy measured in the year after death (age 65 in 2024 → 22.9), reduced by one each year, so 2026 uses **20.9**: $510,000 ÷ 20.9 = **$24,402**.

**The three options, run end-to-end (2026–2050, 6% return, heirs at 32%, in 2026 dollars):**

| Option | After-tax wealth 12/31/2050 | vs. B | Lifetime federal tax (today's $) | Lifetime Medicare (today's $) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B** — RMD only, dump the rest in 2033 | $4,708,755 | — | $1,169,115 | $198,987 |
| **A** — extra $200k in 2026 and 2027 | $4,686,489 | **−$22,266** | $1,149,849 | $203,583 |
| **C** — extra $55k a year, 2026–2033 | **$4,721,638** | **+$12,884** | $1,154,051 | $194,341 |

**Why B is the worst of the two extremes.** Doing nothing concentrates the whole $510,000 into 2033: the final inherited-IRA distribution is $553,600, which stacks on Sam's first real IRA RMDs (his own RMDs begin in 2031) and lifts AGI to $812,275 — through the 24%, 32% and 35% brackets, a $195,139 federal tax bill, and a top IRMAA tier that hits two years later (2035 Medicare of $10,978 per person).

**Why A is worse still.** It saves tax on paper but pays for it: 2026–2027 income jumps into the 22%/24% brackets and kills the OBBBA senior deduction entirely, and the 2026–2027 income spikes set IRMAA tier 2 for 2028–2029 (+$6,060 and +$6,214). The money pulled out early then sits in savings earning taxable interest that is taxed every year at 22–24% and feeds the NIIT for the next two decades.

**Why C wins.** Roughly $55,000 a year keeps the inherited IRA distributions inside the 12%/22% brackets (and preserves part of the senior deduction through 2028), then lets the 2033 deadline distribution be a manageable $146,526 instead of $553,600. It is the only option that lowers both lifetime tax *and* lifetime Medicare premiums — Medicare alone is $5,940 cheaper because 2033's income lands in IRMAA tier 1 rather than tier 4. The edge over B is $12,884, and over A $35,150 — comfortably outside the $1,000 "close call" band.

**Caveats worth knowing.** The prize is small relative to the household: the inherited IRA is a side account next to Sam's $1.68M traditional IRA, whose RMDs from 2031 onward dominate the tax picture, and the projection assumes a flat 6% return for 25 years. The biggest unknowns that could move this are the actual investment return, any tax-exempt muni interest, and the brokerage account's titling (which sets the basis step-up at the first death). Note also that a modest annual Roth conversion of Sam's IRA in 2026–2030 would very likely be worth more than any of these three options — worth modelling next.

PICK: C

text:
## What I found

I ran all three options through the full projection (2026–2050, Sam dying in 2040, survivor filing single afterward), with the 6% return, 2.5% inflation, Arizona-free (no state tax), IRMAA on two-year-lagged MAGI, and the pro-rata rule applied to Sam's $163,000 of IRA basis.

**After-tax wealth at the end of 2050, in today's dollars:**

| Option | After-tax wealth (today's $) | Lifetime federal tax (today's $) | Lifetime Medicare (today's $) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: both at 67 | 2,434,627 | 374,567 | 118,851 |
| B: Sam at 70, Pat at 67 | 2,450,749 | 392,336 | 122,320 |
| **C: B + $180k conversions 2026–29** | **2,708,924** | **265,828** | **99,218** |

**Delaying Sam to 70 (A → B) is a small win: +$16,123.** Waiting raises Sam's benefit to 124% of a $3,490 PIA — $53,097 in 2030, $59,376 in 2031 — and that larger, COLA-bearing benefit lasts as long as *either* spouse lives, because Pat keeps the bigger of the two at Sam's death. But B also pays more lifetime tax (+$30,337) and more Medicare (+$6,199), mostly because the bigger checks drag more of the benefit into taxable income and later push Pat into higher IRMAA tiers. Net, it's barely ahead of claiming at 67 — the delay is a modest, not a dramatic, improvement, and it's sensitive to how long Sam lives.

**The Roth conversions are the real money: +$274,298 over A and +$258,175 over B.** This is not a close call. The reason is the shape of their income: from 2026 to 2029 they have essentially no taxable income (Social Security not started, only ~$33k of interest and dividends, a $35,500+ standard deduction plus a $12,000 senior deduction). That's four years of nearly empty 10%, 12% and 22% brackets — and the senior deduction is still available (it expires after 2028). Converting $180,000 a year fills those brackets at roughly a 12–22% average cost. The alternative is the "do nothing" path, where RMDs starting in 2035 at ~$79,000 (rising to $194,531 by 2050) plus a survivor's single brackets push them into the 22–24% brackets, make 80–95% of Social Security taxable, trigger the 3.8% NIIT, and eventually put Pat in IRMAA tiers 2 and 3 (premiums of $12,760/year by 2050). Option C drains the traditional IRAs down to ~$950k by 2050 and moves the money into Roth, where it grows tax-free, is never subject to RMDs, and keeps Pat in IRMAA tier 0–1 for most of the survivor years.

Two details worth noting: the 2026 conversion is only partly taxable (AGI rises $155,931, not $180,000) because Sam's basis is spread pro rata — about 14% of each conversion comes out tax-free. And the conversion taxes are paid out of savings, which is why the cash account is drawn to zero by 2033; that is the intended trade, since it effectively moves money from a taxable account into a tax-free one.

**Caveats that could move the answer:** the assumed 6% return (a higher return makes converting worth more), the $112,000 spending level, the heirs' tax rate (I valued leftover traditional IRA money at the 10% heirs rate you gave; at 24% converting would look even better), and Sam's health. Also unasked: how the joint brokerage is titled, which matters for the step-up at Sam's death — it's worth only ~$6,300 here, so it doesn't change the ranking.

**Answers to your specific questions:**

- **N1:** In 2026, option B owes **$0** federal income tax (AGI $37,200, wiped out by the $35,500 standard deduction plus the $12,000 senior deduction). Option C owes **$22,255** (AGI $193,131, senior deduction shrinking to $6,824, taxable income $150,807). The difference is **$22,255**.
- **N2:** Sam claims at 70 (February 2030). With the 3.6% COLA in 2027 and 2.5% thereafter, Sam's 2031 benefit is **$59,376** for the year.

PICK: C
N1: 22255
N2: 59376

## What's actually in front of them in 2026

Start with the do-nothing baseline. Under **Option B**, 2026 looks like this: Social Security $69,120, of which $53,694 is taxable, plus the $28,000 pension, $9,000 of interest on savings and $8,550 of dividends. AGI $99,244, MAGI (adding the $20,000 of muni interest) $119,244, standard deduction $35,500, senior deduction $12,000, **taxable income $51,744** and **federal tax $4,790**.

The 0% capital-gain ceiling for a joint return is $98,900 of taxable income, so on paper they have about **$47,000 of "free" room**. It isn't free. Their ordinary income already fills the lower brackets, their Social Security is deep inside the "tax torpedo" zone (85% of it is already taxable, so that part is saturated), and every extra dollar of MAGI above $150,000 claws back 6% per spouse of the new senior deduction. That is why the marginal cost of the room is much higher than the headline 0% suggests.

## Option A — harvest $110,000 of gains

2026 federal tax: **$17,666**. The $12,876 increase breaks down as:

- **+$11,343** on the dividends and gains — they stack on top of ordinary income, so most of the $110,000 lands in the 15% band, not the 0% band;
- **+$607** from the torpedo — taxable Social Security rises from $53,694 to $58,752;
- **+$926** from the senior deduction shrinking from $12,000 to $4,284.

So the "0% harvest" costs about **11.7 cents per dollar harvested**. Worse, MAGI jumps to $234,302, which clears the first IRMAA threshold ($218,000): their 2028 Part B + Part D premiums go from tier 0 to tier 1, +$2,412 of lifetime Medicare. Lifetime tax rises from $400,536 to $407,028 (today's dollars).

And here's the sting: **the higher basis never pays off in this plan.** They never need to sell the brokerage account — it funds nothing, and at the end it's counted at full value (heirs get a step-up). Paying $12,876 now to raise basis on an asset that is never taxed again is pure loss. After-tax wealth: **$3,139,293, i.e. $24,478 worse than doing nothing.**

## Option C — convert $110,000

This is where the pro-rata rule is their friend. Frank's IRA is $830,000 with $172,000 of Form 8606 basis, so only **$88,495 of the $110,000 conversion is taxable** (about $21,505 comes back tax-free). 2026 federal tax: **$21,981**, i.e. **$17,191** more than doing nothing — roughly **19.4% on the taxable slice**. The $17,191 consists of +$13,794 of tax on the conversion itself, +$1,113 from the torpedo, +$1,130 from the senior deduction ($12,000 → $6,864) and +$1,154 because the conversion pushes their qualified dividends out of the 0% band.

Why that is a good trade:

- They are paying ~19% now to avoid **22% later** — and "later" starts in 2035, when Frank's RMDs begin. In the do-nothing plan the 2035 RMD is $63,329 and taxable income jumps to $141,620 (tax $17,042, up from $6,810 the year before). With the conversion, 2035's RMD is $56,203 and tax is $15,430.
- **It fits under the first IRMAA cliff.** MAGI is $212,797, under $218,000 — so 2028 premiums stay at tier 0, unlike Option A.
- Lifetime federal tax falls from $400,536 to **$375,213** (today's dollars) with no extra Medicare cost, and there is more left in Roth (Frank's Roth ends at $595,598 vs $150,215).

After-tax wealth: **$3,203,401 — $39,630 more than B and $64,108 more than A.** Not close.

## The verdict and the caveats

The room should go to the **Roth conversion**. The 0% capital-gains bracket is a red herring here: their Social Security torpedo, the senior-deduction phase-out and the IRMAA cliff mean the room costs 11.7% in real tax and buys them a basis step-up they will never use. The conversion, by contrast, is the last cheap window — the senior deduction disappears after 2028 and RMDs start in 2035, and the $172,000 of basis makes it unusually efficient. One practical note: they can't do both — $110,000 of gains *and* a $110,000 conversion would put MAGI near $308,000 and into IRMAA tier 2.

Two things to verify before they file: the **$172,000 Form 8606 basis** on Frank's IRA (every dollar of basis verified saves 22 cents of conversion tax), and the **heirs' bracket** — if the kids are in the 12% bracket the conversion's edge shrinks by about $12,000, though it still wins.

## What the muni bonds actually do

The tax-exempt interest doesn't block a Roth conversion — but it isn't invisible either. It counts in **provisional income** for taxing Social Security and in **MAGI** for IRMAA. So the $24,000 of muni interest makes every extra dollar of conversion more expensive than the bracket alone suggests.

For 2026, the conversion also runs through the pro-rata rule: Walt's IRA has $46,000 of basis out of $1,080,000, so of a $135,500 gross conversion only about $129,700 is taxable — the rest is a return of his after-tax money.

**Option A vs. C, 2026 (from the projection):**
- AGI $78,490 → $217,505; MAGI for IRMAA $102,490 → $241,505
- Taxable Social Security $44,590 → $53,550 (the "tax torpedo" — more of their benefits become taxable)
- Senior deduction $12,000 → $3,899 (the 6%-of-MAGI phase-out, figured per person)
- Dividends/gains pushed out of the 0% capital-gain band: $0 → $324 of tax
- Federal tax $2,964 → $28,456, paid out of the savings account

**The IRMAA consequence shows up in 2028**, because 2026 income sets those premiums: MAGI of $241,505 crosses the $230,000 joint threshold, so both spouses move from tier 0 to tier 1 — Part B $298.50 + Part D surcharge $15.20 instead of the $213.20 standard, i.e. $1,206 more per person for the year.

**Over the whole run (2026–2050, today's dollars):**

| Plan | After-tax wealth | vs. C |
|---|---|---|
| C — no conversion | $3,328,602 | — |
| B — convert $126,500 | $3,386,455 | +$57,853 |
| A — convert $135,500 | $3,389,555 | +$60,953 |

A also cuts lifetime tax by $67,534 and lifetime Medicare by $9,166 versus doing nothing, and it lowers RMDs enough that the couple stays out of the top IRMAA tiers in the late 2040s. A beats B by about $3,100, so this isn't a close call — converting the larger amount inside the 22% bracket is the better trade, even after paying the 2028 surcharge and the torpedo.

Two things would change the answer: a materially lower expected return (at 4%, B would edge out A), and the heirs' tax bracket (at 12%, converting pays much less — I assumed 32%).

PICK: A
